[{:db/id 17592186152256 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-071418af-96d7-52c9-8845-42c31b88cc12" "question-bb353c96-604c-5c65-9adf-47096b9ec124" "question-22db406c-85ef-5a5a-ab22-d062645b4362" "question-3c1db003-08b1-562e-8980-51389652bb7b" "question-a9e1ee25-17a0-56ec-9f69-bcad0ae7d0cc"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186151849 :question/problem "Consider the equivalence relation $\sim$ on $\mathbb{Z},$ defined by $x \sim y$ if $12 \,|\, (x-y).$ Which of the following are in the equivalence class $[9]?$

I. $9$

II. $21$

III. $22$" :question/worked-solution "The equivalence class $[9]$ consists of the elements that are equivalent to $9$ under the given equivalence relation. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[9] & ={x\in Z\,:\,x∼9} \\  & ={x\in Z\,:\,12\,|\,(x-9)} \\  & ={x\in Z\,:\,x=9+12k,k\in Z} \\  & ={…,-15,-3,9,21,33,…}.\end{aligned}
$$

We see that $9$ and $21$ are in $[9],$ while $22$ is not.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152257 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-46852a07-1e77-54f8-9037-1f17a12c391f" "question-c88f13fc-8d9b-5fc7-ac75-4d5797158af8" "question-fd41a54f-8627-52be-9ff1-ad5548f86090" "question-9d844129-f571-5c80-934e-cfc1faad53cf"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186151851 :question/problem "Consider the equivalence relation $\sim$ on $\mathbb{R},$ defined by $x \sim y$ if $\sin x = \sin y.$ Which of the following equivalence classes contain the element $\dfrac{\pi}{2}?$

I. $\left[\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right]$

II. $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$

III. $\left[-\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right]$" :question/worked-solution "We have $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \in [x]$ if $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \sim x.$ Using the definition of the given equivalence relation, we require

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ 1 & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡x & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now consider each of the given equivalence classes.

- $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \not\in \left[\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right]$ because $\sin\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) =-1\neq 1 \quad \color{red}\times$

- $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \not\in \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ because $\sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) =-1\neq 1 \quad \color{red}\times$

- $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \in \left[-\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right]$ because $\sin \left(-\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) = 1  \quad \color{green}\checkmark$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only"." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152258 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d047cc89-db39-59a7-988f-ed7cc91aeaba" "question-67dde538-2d6b-5e8f-8a86-3af3686c7b06" "question-f558440e-fbbe-5f40-9ac9-a9ba45c6c38a" "question-cd31c5ed-d4ae-58a5-ab4f-af985ca907a3" "question-d77f9f0f-9817-528d-99c4-631fe49372a3"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186151852 :question/problem "Consider the equivalence relation $\sim$ on the set $A = \{0, 1, 2, \ldots, 9\},$ defined by $a \sim b$ if $\textrm{i}^a = \textrm{i}^b,$ where $\textrm{i}$ is the imaginary unit in $\mathbb{C}.$  How many distinct equivalence classes does $\sim$ partition $A$ into?" :question/worked-solution "The equivalence classes of $\sim$ partition $A,$ meaning that any element $a \in A$ belongs to exactly one distinct equivalence class.

So, we compute equivalence classes until all the elements of $A$ have been placed into an equivalence class.

$$
\begin{aligned}[0] & ={a\in A∣a∼0} \\  & ={a\in A∣{\text{i}}^{a}={\text{i}}^{0}} \\  & ={a\in A∣{\text{i}}^{a}=1} \\  & ={0,4,8} \\  \\ [1] & ={a\in A∣a∼1} \\  & ={a\in A∣{\text{i}}^{a}={\text{i}}^{1}} \\  & ={a\in A∣{\text{i}}^{a}=\text{i}} \\  & ={1,5,9} \\  \\ [2] & ={a\in A∣a∼2} \\  & ={a\in A∣{\text{i}}^{a}={\text{i}}^{2}} \\  & ={a\in A∣{\text{i}}^{a}=-1} \\  & ={2,6} \\  \\ [3] & ={a\in A∣a∼3} \\  & ={a\in A∣{\text{i}}^{a}={\text{i}}^{3}} \\  & ={a\in A∣{\text{i}}^{a}=-\text{i}} \\  & ={3,7}\end{aligned}
$$

Each element of $A$ has been placed into an equivalence class, so we are done.

We have $4$ distinct equivalence classes:

$$
[0] = \{ 0, 4, 8 \} , \quad [1] = \{ 1, 5, 9 \}, \quad [2] = \{ 2, 6 \}, \quad [3] = \{ 3, 7 \}.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-071418af-96d7-52c9-8845-42c31b88cc12" :question/id #uuid "071418af-96d7-52c9-8845-42c31b88cc12" :question/math-academy-id "q-77200" :question/problem "Consider the equivalence relation $∼$ on $R,$ defined by $x∼y$ if ${x}^{3}={y}^{3}.$ Which of the following are in the equivalence class $[8]?$

I. $-2$

II. $2$

III. $8$" :question/worked-solution "The equivalence class $[8]$ consists of the elements that are equivalent to $8$ under the given equivalence relation. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[8] & ={x\in R\,|\,x∼8} \\  & ={x\in R\,|\,{x}^{3}={8}^{3}} \\  & ={x\in R\,|\,x=8} \\  & ={8}.\end{aligned}
$$

We see that $8$ is in $[8],$ while $-2$ and $2$ are not.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only"." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-fe48b365-00e3-52fe-9ee6-28adef726d37"] :db/ensure $$
\begin{aligned}[-8] & ={x\in R\,|\,x∼-8} \\  & ={x\in R\,|\,\sqrt[3]{x}=\sqrt[3]{-8}} \\  & ={x\in R\,|\,\sqrt[3]{x}=-2} \\  & ={-8}.\end{aligned}
$$

We see that $-8$ is in $[-8],$ while $8$ and $2$ are not.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only"." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-4af3f260-723a-5617-9400-73aac1989855"] :db/ensure :question/problem "Consider the equivalence relation $∼$ on $C,$ defined by $x∼y$ if ${x}^{2}={y}^{2}.$ Which of the following are in the equivalence class $[-4]?$

II. $4$

III. $4\text{i}$" :question/worked-solution "The equivalence class $[-4]$ consists of the elements that are equivalent to $-4$ under the given equivalence relation. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[-4] & ={x\in C\,|\,x∼-4} \\  & ={x\in C\,|\,{x}^{2}=(-4)^{2}} \\  & ={x\in C\,|\,{x}^{2}=16} \\  & ={-4,4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We see that $-4$ and $4$ are in $[-4],$ while $4\text{i}$ is not.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only"." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-427832c3-ff8d-5621-b856-408a0605c9f1"] :db/ensure :question/problem "Consider the equivalence relation $∼$ on $R,$ defined by $x∼y$ if $\operatorname{cos}⁡x=\operatorname{cos}⁡y.$ Which of the following are in the equivalence class $[0]?$

I. $2\pi $

II. $3\pi $

III. $\frac{\pi }{2}$" :question/worked-solution "The equivalence class $[0]$ consists of the elements that are equivalent to $0$ under the given equivalence relation. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[0] & ={x\in R\,|\,x∼0} \\  & ={x\in R\,|\,\operatorname{cos}⁡x=\operatorname{cos}⁡0} \\  & ={x\in R\,|\,\operatorname{cos}⁡x=1} \\  & ={…,-4\pi ,-2\pi ,0,2\pi ,4\pi ,…}.\end{aligned}
$$

We see that $2\pi $ is in $[0],$ while $3\pi $ and $\frac{\pi }{2}$ are not.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-11f848d9-afc8-5368-b1fd-07597c4b200a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-11f848d9-afc8-5368-b1fd-07597c4b200a" :answer-field/id #uuid "11f848d9-afc8-5368-b1fd-07597c4b200a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-e261b60f-981d-5dea-add0-42767006246e" :answer-field/choices ["answer-beda1346-455c-59a5-b6e2-690d2703d950" "answer-e261b60f-981d-5dea-add0-42767006246e" "answer-641a1fbc-83f5-514f-b0d5-77a3f28046d6" "answer-d8687927-2b83-51b2-aa18-5333115cbc1d" "answer-3fb079ab-f666-5cc0-acd0-dc79af768608"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-beda1346-455c-59a5-b6e2-690d2703d950" :answer/id #uuid "beda1346-455c-59a5-b6e2-690d2703d950" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e261b60f-981d-5dea-add0-42767006246e" :answer/id #uuid "e261b60f-981d-5dea-add0-42767006246e" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-641a1fbc-83f5-514f-b0d5-77a3f28046d6" :answer/id #uuid "641a1fbc-83f5-514f-b0d5-77a3f28046d6" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d8687927-2b83-51b2-aa18-5333115cbc1d" :answer/id #uuid "d8687927-2b83-51b2-aa18-5333115cbc1d" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3fb079ab-f666-5cc0-acd0-dc79af768608" :answer/id #uuid "3fb079ab-f666-5cc0-acd0-dc79af768608" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152754 :question/problem "Consider the equivalence relation $∼$ on $C,$ defined by $x∼y$ if ${x}^{4}={y}^{4}.$ Which of the following equivalence classes contain the element $i?$

I. $[-1]$

II. $[-i]$

III. $[2i]$" :question/worked-solution "We have $i\in [x]$ if $i∼x.$ Using the definition of the given equivalence relation, we require

$$
\begin{aligned}{i}^{4} & ={x}^{4} \\ 1 & ={x}^{4} \\ {x}^{4} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now consider each of the given equivalence classes.

- $i\in [-1]$ because $(-1)^{4}=1\,✓$

- $i\in [-i]$ because $(-i)^{4}=1\,✓$

- $i\notin [2i]$ because $(2i)^{4}=16\ne 1\,\times $

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only"." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186151031 :answer-field/correct 17592186151034 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-46852a07-1e77-54f8-9037-1f17a12c391f" :question/id #uuid "46852a07-1e77-54f8-9037-1f17a12c391f" :question/math-academy-id "q-221767" :question/problem "Consider the equivalence relation $∼$ on $R,$ defined by $x∼y$ if $\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi y.$ Which of the following equivalence classes contain the element $3$

I. $[0]$

II. $[1]$

III. $[2]$" :question/worked-solution "We have $3\in [x]$ if $3∼x.$ Using the definition of the given equivalence relation, we require

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi \cdot 3 & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi x \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡3\pi  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi x \\ -1 & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi x \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi x & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now consider each of the given equivalence classes.

- $3\notin [0]$ because $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 0)=1\ne -1\,\times $

- $3\in [1]$ because $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 1)=-1\,✓$

the equivalence relation $∼$ on the set $A={0,\,\pm 1,\,\pm 2},$ defined by $x∼y$ if $\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}=\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}}.$ How many distinct equivalence classes does $∼$ partition $A$ into?" :question/worked-solution "The equivalence classes of $∼$ partition $A,$ meaning that any element $a\in A$ belongs to exactly one distinct equivalence class.

So, we compute equivalence classes until all the elements of $A$ have been placed into an equivalence class.

$$
\begin{aligned}[0] & ={x\in A∣x∼0} \\  & ={x\in A∣\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}=\sqrt[3]{{0}^{2}}} \\  & ={x\in A∣\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}=0} \\  & ={x\in A∣{x}^{2}=0} \\  & ={0} \\  \\ [1] & ={x\in A∣x∼1} \\  & ={x\in A∣\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}=\sqrt[3]{{1}^{2}}} \\  & ={x\in A∣\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}=1} \\  & ={x\in A∣{x}^{2}=1} \\  & ={-1,1} \\  \\ [2] & ={x\in A∣x∼2} \\  & ={x\in A∣\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}=\sqrt[3]{{2}^{2}}} \\  & ={x\in A∣\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}=\sqrt[3]{4}} \\  & ={x\in A∣{x}^{2}=4} \\  & ={-2,2} \\ \end{aligned}
$$

All of the elements of $A$ have been placed into an equivalence class, so we are done.

We have $3$ distinct equivalence classes:

$$
[0]={0},\,[1]={-1,1},\,[2]={-2,2}.
$$

Notice that the equivalence classes form a partition of $A,$ as expected." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b2bb8163-4fc3-598a-b15f-be6314a5e713"] the equivalence relation $∼$ on the set $A={0,\,\pm 1,\,\pm 2,\,\pm 3,\,\pm 4},$ defined by $x∼y$ if ${x}^{2}={y}^{2}.$ How many distinct equivalence classes does $∼$ partition $A$ into?" :question/worked-solution "The equivalence classes of $∼$ partition $A,$ meaning that any element $a\in A$ belongs to exactly one distinct equivalence class.

So, we compute equivalence classes until all the elements of $A$ have been placed into an equivalence class.

$$
\begin{aligned}[0] & ={x\in A∣x∼0} \\  & ={x\in A∣{x}^{2}={0}^{2}} \\  & ={0} \\  \\ [1] & ={x\in A∣x∼1} \\  & ={x\in A∣{x}^{2}={1}^{2}} \\  & ={x\in A∣{x}^{2}=1} \\  & ={-1,1} \\  \\ [2] & ={x\in A∣x∼2} \\  & ={x\in A∣{x}^{2}={2}^{2}} \\  & ={x\in A∣{x}^{2}=4} \\  & ={-2,2} \\  \\ [3] & ={x\in A∣x∼3} \\  & ={x\in A∣{x}^{2}={3}^{2}} \\  & ={x\in A∣{x}^{2}=9} \\  & ={-3,3} \\  \\ [4] & ={x\in A∣x∼4} \\  & ={x\in A∣{x}^{2}={4}^{2}} \\  & ={x\in A∣{x}^{2}=16} \\  & ={-4,4} \\ \end{aligned}
$$

All of the elements of $A$ have been placed into an equivalence class, so we are done.

We have $5$ distinct equivalence classes:

$$
[0]={0},\,[1]={-1,1},\,[2]={-2,2},\,[3]={-3,3},\,[4]={-4,4}.
$$

Notice that the equivalence classes form a partition of $A,$ as expected." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d8ae37cc-586d-5f42-83a1-41443720bcf7"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d8ae37cc-586d-5f42-83a1-41443720bcf7" :answer-field/id #uuid "d8ae37cc-586d-5f42-83a1-41443720bcf7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-f38111d5-9586-53b6-857b-55f2afbf3761" :answer-field/choices ["answer-11e08c36-c324-5321-9cf4-a44ee441312d" "answer-934a840c-bff8-5510-9234-70b0bf17c493" "answer-be425907-329d-5a10-b5db-ab365fa81476" "answer-ca907d65-9e23-5d93-9273-436e6ef31767" "answer-f38111d5-9586-53b6-857b-55f2afbf3761"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-11e08c36-c324-5321-9cf4-a44ee441312d" :answer/id #uuid "11e08c36-c324-5321-9cf4-a44ee441312d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-934a840c-bff8-5510-9234-70b0bf17c493" :answer/id #uuid "934a840c-bff8-5510-9234-70b0bf17c493" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "16" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-be425907-329d-5a10-b5db-ab365fa81476" :answer/id #uuid "be425907-329d-5a10-b5db-ab365fa81476" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "25" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ca907d65-9e23-5d93-9273-436e6ef31767" :answer/id #uuid "ca907d65-9e23-5d93-9273-436e6ef31767" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f38111d5-9586-53b6-857b-55f2afbf3761" :answer/id #uuid "f38111d5-9586-53b6-857b-55f2afbf3761" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186153457 :tutorial/content "Recall that the residue class of $a$ modulo $n,$ denoted $[a]_n,$ is the set of integers that are congruent to $a$ modulo $n.$

$$
[a]_n = \big\{ x \in \mathbb{Z} \: | \: x \equiv a \,  \: (\text{mod}\:n) \big\}
$$

For example:

- The residue class of $0$ modulo $2$ corresponds to the even integers because all even integers have a remainder of $0$ when divided by $2.$

$$
\begin{aligned}[0]_{2}={0,\,\pm 2,\,\pm 4,\,…}\end{aligned}
$$

- On the other hand, the residue class of $1$ modulo $2$ corresponds to the odd integers because all odd integers have a remainder of $1$ when divided by $2.$

$$
\begin{aligned}[1]_{2}={\,\pm 1,\,\pm 3,\,\pm 5,\,…}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the residue classes $[0]_2$ and $[1]_2$ *partition* the integers, meaning that any integer belongs either to $[0]_2$ or $[1]_2,$ but never both.

![](images/89/8932542ec22de980b3b2e1a5a11a3edf2250efc7ea4f1ca64ca35aa4031c63c9.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186153458 :tutorial/content "A residue class is a particular type of a more general object called an **equivalence class.**

Given an equivalence relation $\sim$ on a set $A,$ the equivalence class of an element $a \in A,$ denoted $[a],$ consists of all the elements of $A$ that are equivalent to $a.$

$$
[a] = \{ x \in A \, | \, x \sim a \}
$$

Since any equivalence relation is symmetric, we can also write

$$
[a] = \{ x \in A \, | \, a \sim x \}.
$$

For example, consider the equivalence relation $\sim$ on $\mathbb{Z}$ defined by $a \sim b$ if and only if $|a|=|b|.$ 

Under this relation, two integers are equivalent if they have the same absolute value. The first few equivalence classes are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[0] & ={a\in Z∣a∼0} \\  & ={a\in Z∣|a|=|0|} \\  & ={a\in Z∣|a|=0} \\  & ={0} \\  \\ [1] & ={a\in Z∣a∼1} \\  & ={a\in Z∣|a|=|1|} \\  & ={a\in Z∣|a|=1} \\  & ={\pm 1} \\  \\ [2] & ={a\in Z∣a∼2} \\  & ={a\in Z∣|a|=|2|} \\  & ={a\in Z∣|a|=2} \\  & ={\pm 2} \\  \\ [3] & ={a\in Z∣a∼3} \\  & ={a\in Z∣|a|=|3|} \\  & ={a\in Z∣|a|=3} \\  & ={\pm 3} \\  & \,⋮\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- Equivalence relations can have a finite or infinite number of equivalence classes. This particular equivalence relation has an infinite number of equivalence classes.

- For equivalence classes containing more than one element, we can use any element to represent the class. For example, $[1]$ and $[-1]$ represent the same equivalence class." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186153480 :tutorial/content "The properties of residue classes generalize to equivalence classes. Let's list some of them:

- If $a \sim b$ then $[a]=[b].$ This allows us to pick any element of a class as its representative.

- On the other hand, two distinct equivalence classes have an empty intersection: 

$$
a \not\sim b
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
[a] \cap [b] = \emptyset
$$

- The residue classes form a partition of $A.$ Moreover, $A$ can be constructed from the (disjoint) union of all distinct equivalence classes:

$$
A = \bigcup_{i\in I}\,[a]_i
$$

where $[a]_i$ denotes the $i$'th residue class and $I$ is an index set spanning all possible classes.

Consider once again the equivalence relation $\sim$ on $\mathbb{Z}$ defined by $a \sim b$ if and only if $|a|=|b|.$ We found that the equivalence classes were as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[0] & ={0} \\ [1] & ={\pm 1} \\ [2] & ={\pm 2} \\ [3] & ={\pm 3} \\  & ⋮\end{aligned}
$$

These equivalence classes form a partition of the set of integers:

$$
\big\{[0], [1], [2],\ldots\big\}
$$

Moreover, the integers can be constructed from the disjoint union of these classes:

$$
\begin{aligned}Z & =[0]\cup [1]\cup [2]\cup ⋯ \\  & ={0}\cup {\pm 1}\cup {\pm 2}\cup ⋯\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152337 :activity/expected-seconds 660.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

{"source" ":org/Math-Academy" "forms" [{:db/id 17592186152256 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-071418af-96d7-52c9-8845-42c31b88cc12" "question-bb353c96-604c-5c65-9adf-47096b9ec124" "question-22db406c-85ef-5a5a-ab22-d062645b4362" "question-3c1db003-08b1-562e-8980-51389652bb7b" "question-a9e1ee25-17a0-56ec-9f69-bcad0ae7d0cc"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186151849 :question/problem "Consider the equivalence relation $\sim$ on $\mathbb{Z},$ defined by $x \sim y$ if $12 \,|\, (x-y).$ Which of the following are in the equivalence class $[9]?$

I. $9$

II. $21$

III. $22$" :question/worked-solution "The equivalence class $[9]$ consists of the elements that are equivalent to $9$ under the given equivalence relation. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[9] & ={x\in Z\,:\,x∼9} \\  & ={x\in Z\,:\,12\,|\,(x-9)} \\  & ={x\in Z\,:\,x=9+12k,k\in Z} \\  & ={…,-15,-3,9,21,33,…}.\end{aligned}
$$

We see that $9$ and $21$ are in $[9],$ while $22$ is not.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152257 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-46852a07-1e77-54f8-9037-1f17a12c391f" "question-c88f13fc-8d9b-5fc7-ac75-4d5797158af8" "question-fd41a54f-8627-52be-9ff1-ad5548f86090" "question-9d844129-f571-5c80-934e-cfc1faad53cf"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186151851 :question/problem "Consider the equivalence relation $\sim$ on $\mathbb{R},$ defined by $x \sim y$ if $\sin x = \sin y.$ Which of the following equivalence classes contain the element $\dfrac{\pi}{2}?$

I. $\left[\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right]$

II. $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$

III. $\left[-\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right]$" :question/worked-solution "We have $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \in [x]$ if $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \sim x.$ Using the definition of the given equivalence relation, we require

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ 1 & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡x & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now consider each of the given equivalence classes.

- $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \not\in \left[\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right]$ because $\sin\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) =-1\neq 1 \quad \color{red}\times$

- $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \not\in \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ because $\sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) =-1\neq 1 \quad \color{red}\times$

- $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \in \left[-\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right]$ because $\sin \left(-\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) = 1  \quad \color{green}\checkmark$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only"." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152258 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d047cc89-db39-59a7-988f-ed7cc91aeaba" "question-67dde538-2d6b-5e8f-8a86-3af3686c7b06" "question-f558440e-fbbe-5f40-9ac9-a9ba45c6c38a" "question-cd31c5ed-d4ae-58a5-ab4f-af985ca907a3" "question-d77f9f0f-9817-528d-99c4-631fe49372a3"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186151852 :question/problem "Consider the equivalence relation $\sim$ on the set $A = \{0, 1, 2, \ldots, 9\},$ defined by $a \sim b$ if $\textrm{i}^a = \textrm{i}^b,$ where $\textrm{i}$ is the imaginary unit in $\mathbb{C}.$  How many distinct equivalence classes does $\sim$ partition $A$ into?" :question/worked-solution "The equivalence classes of $\sim$ partition $A,$ meaning that any element $a \in A$ belongs to exactly one distinct equivalence class.

So, we compute equivalence classes until all the elements of $A$ have been placed into an equivalence class.

$$
\begin{aligned}[0] & ={a\in A∣a∼0} \\  & ={a\in A∣{\text{i}}^{a}={\text{i}}^{0}} \\  & ={a\in A∣{\text{i}}^{a}=1} \\  & ={0,4,8} \\  \\ [1] & ={a\in A∣a∼1} \\  & ={a\in A∣{\text{i}}^{a}={\text{i}}^{1}} \\  & ={a\in A∣{\text{i}}^{a}=\text{i}} \\  & ={1,5,9} \\  \\ [2] & ={a\in A∣a∼2} \\  & ={a\in A∣{\text{i}}^{a}={\text{i}}^{2}} \\  & ={a\in A∣{\text{i}}^{a}=-1} \\  & ={2,6} \\  \\ [3] & ={a\in A∣a∼3} \\  & ={a\in A∣{\text{i}}^{a}={\text{i}}^{3}} \\  & ={a\in A∣{\text{i}}^{a}=-\text{i}} \\  & ={3,7}\end{aligned}
$$

Each element of $A$ has been placed into an equivalence class, so we are done.

We have $4$ distinct equivalence classes:

$$
[0] = \{ 0, 4, 8 \} , \quad [1] = \{ 1, 5, 9 \}, \quad [2] = \{ 2, 6 \}, \quad [3] = \{ 3, 7 \}.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-071418af-96d7-52c9-8845-42c31b88cc12" :question/id #uuid "071418af-96d7-52c9-8845-42c31b88cc12" :question/math-academy-id "q-77200" :question/problem "Consider the equivalence relation $∼$ on $R,$ defined by $x∼y$ if ${x}^{3}={y}^{3}.$ Which of the following are in the equivalence class $[8]?$

I. $-2$

II. $2$

III. $8$" :question/worked-solution "The equivalence class $[8]$ consists of the elements that are equivalent to $8$ under the given equivalence relation. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[8] & ={x\in R\,|\,x∼8} \\  & ={x\in R\,|\,{x}^{3}={8}^{3}} \\  & ={x\in R\,|\,x=8} \\  & ={8}.\end{aligned}
$$

We see that $8$ is in $[8],$ while $-2$ and $2$ are not.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only"." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-fe48b365-00e3-52fe-9ee6-28adef726d37"] :db/ensure $$
\begin{aligned}[5] & ={x\in Z\,:\,x∼5} \\  & ={x\in Z\,:\,7\,|\,(x-5)} \\  & ={x\in Z\,:\,x=5+7k,k\in Z} \\  & ={…,-9,-2,5,12,19,…}.\end{aligned}

$$
[a]_n = \big\{ x \in \mathbb{Z} \: | \: x \equiv a \,  \: (\text{mod}\:n) \big\}
$$

For example:

- The residue class of $0$ modulo $2$ corresponds to the even integers because all even integers have a remainder of $0$ when divided by $2.$

$$
\begin{aligned}[0]_{2}={0,\,\pm 2,\,\pm 4,\,…}\end{aligned}
$$

- On the other hand, the residue class of $1$ modulo $2$ corresponds to the odd integers because all odd integers have a remainder of $1$ when divided by $2.$

$$
\begin{aligned}[1]_{2}={\,\pm 1,\,\pm 3,\,\pm 5,\,…}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the residue classes $[0]_2$ and $[1]_2$ *partition* the integers, meaning that any integer belongs either to $[0]_2$ or $[1]_2,$ but never both.

![](images/89/8932542ec22de980b3b2e1a5a11a3edf2250efc7ea4f1ca64ca35aa4031c63c9.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186153458 :tutorial/content "A residue class is a particular type of a more general object called an **equivalence class.**

Given an equivalence relation $\sim$ on a set $A,$ the equivalence class of an element $a \in A,$ denoted $[a],$ consists of all the elements of $A$ that are equivalent to $a.$

$$
[a] = \{ x \in A \, | \, x \sim a \}
$$

Since any equivalence relation is symmetric, we can also write

$$
[a] = \{ x \in A \, | \, a \sim x \}.
$$

For example, consider the equivalence relation $\sim$ on $\mathbb{Z}$ defined by $a \sim b$ if and only if $|a|=|b|.$ 

Under this relation, two integers are equivalent if they have the same absolute value. The first few equivalence classes are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[0] & ={a\in Z∣a∼0} \\  & ={a\in Z∣|a|=|0|} \\  & ={a\in Z∣|a|=0} \\  & ={0} \\  \\ [1] & ={a\in Z∣a∼1} \\  & ={a\in Z∣|a|=|1|} \\  & ={a\in Z∣|a|=1} \\  & ={\pm 1} \\  \\ [2] & ={a\in Z∣a∼2} \\  & ={a\in Z∣|a|=|2|} \\  & ={a\in Z∣|a|=2} \\  & ={\pm 2} \\  \\ [3] & ={a\in Z∣a∼3} \\  & ={a\in Z∣|a|=|3|} \\  & ={a\in Z∣|a|=3} \\  & ={\pm 3} \\  & \,⋮\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- Equivalence relations can have a finite or infinite number of equivalence classes. This particular equivalence relation has an infinite number of equivalence classes.

- For equivalence classes containing more than one element, we can use any element to represent the class. For example, $[1]$ and $[-1]$ represent the same equivalence class." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186153480 :tutorial/content "The properties of residue classes generalize to equivalence classes. Let's list some of them:

- If $a \sim b$ then $[a]=[b].$ This allows us to pick any element of a class as its representative.

- On the other hand, two distinct equivalence classes have an empty intersection: 

$$
a \not\sim b
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
[a] \cap [b] = \emptyset
$$

- The residue classes form a partition of $A.$ Moreover, $A$ can be constructed from the (disjoint) union of all distinct equivalence classes:

$$
A = \bigcup_{i\in I}\,[a]_i
$$

where $[a]_i$ denotes the $i$'th residue class and $I$ is an index set spanning all possible classes.

Consider once again the equivalence relation $\sim$ on $\mathbb{Z}$ defined by $a \sim b$ if and only if $|a|=|b|.$ We found that the equivalence classes were as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[0] & ={0} \\ [1] & ={\pm 1} \\ [2] & ={\pm 2} \\ [3] & ={\pm 3} \\  & ⋮\end{aligned}
$$

These equivalence classes form a partition of the set of integers:

$$
\big\{[0], [1], [2],\ldots\big\}
$$

Moreover, the integers can be constructed from the disjoint union of these classes:

$$
\begin{aligned}Z & =[0]\cup [1]\cup [2]\cup ⋯ \\  & ={0}\cup {\pm 1}\cup {\pm 2}\cup ⋯\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152337 :activity/expected-seconds 660.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}] "assertions" [[17592186151849 :question/problem "Consider the equivalence relation $\sim$ on $\mathbb{Z},$ defined by $x \sim y$ if $12 \,|\, (x-y).$ Which of the following are in the equivalence class $[9]?$

I. $9$

II. $21$

III. $22$"] [17592186151849 :question/worked-solution "The equivalence class $[9]$ consists of the elements that are equivalent to $9$ under the given equivalence relation. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[9] & ={x\in Z\,:\,x∼9} \\  & ={x\in Z\,:\,12\,|\,(x-9)} \\  & ={x\in Z\,:\,x=9+12k,k\in Z} \\  & ={…,-15,-3,9,21,33,…}.\end{aligned}
$$

We see that $9$ and $21$ are in $[9],$ while $22$ is not.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only.""] [17592186151851 :question/problem "Consider the equivalence relation $\sim$ on $\mathbb{R},$ defined by $x \sim y$ if $\sin x = \sin y.$ Which of the following equivalence classes contain the element $\dfrac{\pi}{2}?$

I. $\left[\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right]$

II. $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$

III. $\left[-\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right]$"] [17592186151851 :question/worked-solution "We have $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \in [x]$ if $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \sim x.$ Using the definition of the given equivalence relation, we require

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ 1 & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡x & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now consider each of the given equivalence classes.

- $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \not\in \left[\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right]$ because $\sin\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) =-1\neq 1 \quad \color{red}\times$

- $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \not\in \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ because $\sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) =-1\neq 1 \quad \color{red}\times$

- $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \in \left[-\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right]$ because $\sin \left(-\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) = 1  \quad \color{green}\checkmark$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only"."] [17592186151852 :question/problem "Consider the equivalence relation $\sim$ on the set $A = \{0, 1, 2, \ldots, 9\},$ defined by $a \sim b$ if $\textrm{i}^a = \textrm{i}^b,$ where $\textrm{i}$ is the imaginary unit in $\mathbb{C}.$  How many distinct equivalence classes does $\sim$ partition $A$ into?"] [17592186151852 :question/worked-solution "The equivalence classes of $\sim$ partition $A,$ meaning that any element $a \in A$ belongs to exactly one distinct equivalence class.

So, we compute equivalence classes until all the elements of $A$ have been placed into an equivalence class.

$$
\begin{aligned}[0] & ={a\in A∣a∼0} \\  & ={a\in A∣{\text{i}}^{a}={\text{i}}^{0}} \\  & ={a\in A∣{\text{i}}^{a}=1} \\  & ={0,4,8} \\  \\ [1] & ={a\in A∣a∼1} \\  & ={a\in A∣{\text{i}}^{a}={\text{i}}^{1}} \\  & ={a\in A∣{\text{i}}^{a}=\text{i}} \\  & ={1,5,9} \\  \\ [2] & ={a\in A∣a∼2} \\  & ={a\in A∣{\text{i}}^{a}={\text{i}}^{2}} \\  & ={a\in A∣{\text{i}}^{a}=-1} \\  & ={2,6} \\  \\ [3] & ={a\in A∣a∼3} \\  & ={a\in A∣{\text{i}}^{a}={\text{i}}^{3}} \\  & ={a\in A∣{\text{i}}^{a}=-\text{i}} \\  & ={3,7}\end{aligned}
$$

Each element of $A$ has been placed into an equivalence class, so we are done.

We have $4$ distinct equivalence classes:

$$
[0] = \{ 0, 4, 8 \} , \quad [1] = \{ 1, 5, 9 \}, \quad [2] = \{ 2, 6 \}, \quad [3] = \{ 3, 7 \}.
$$"] ["question-071418af-96d7-52c9-8845-42c31b88cc12" :question/id #uuid "071418af-96d7-52c9-8845-42c31b88cc12"] ["question-071418af-96d7-52c9-8845-42c31b88cc12" :question/math-academy-id "q-77200"] ["question-071418af-96d7-52c9-8845-42c31b88cc12" :question/problem "Consider the equivalence relation $∼$ on $R,$ defined by $x∼y$ if ${x}^{3}={y}^{3}.$ Which of the following are in the equivalence class $[8]?$

II. $2$

III. $8$"] ["question-071418af-96d7-52c9-8845-42c31b88cc12" :question/worked-solution "The equivalence class $[8]$ consists of the elements that are equivalent to $8$ under the given equivalence relation. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[8] & ={x\in R\,|\,x∼8} \\  & ={x\in R\,|\,{x}^{3}={8}^{3}} \\  & ={x\in R\,|\,x=8} \\  & ={8}.\end{aligned}
$$

We see that $8$ is in $[8],$ while $-2$ and $2$ are not.

$$

We see that $2\pi $ is in $[0],$ while $3\pi $ and $\frac{\pi }{2}$ are not.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only"."] [17592186152754 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] [17592186151031 :answer-field/correct 17592186151034] ["question-46852a07-1e77-54f8-9037-1f17a12c391f" :question/id #uuid "46852a07-1e77-54f8-9037-1f17a12c391f"] ["question-46852a07-1e77-54f8-9037-1f17a12c391f" :question/math-academy-id "q-221767"] ["question-46852a07-1e77-54f8-9037-1f17a12c391f" :question/problem "Consider the equivalence relation $∼$ on $R,$ defined by $x∼y$ if $\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi y.$ Which of the following equivalence classes contain the element $3$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi \cdot 3 & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi x \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡3\pi  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi x \\ -1 & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi x \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi x & =-1.\end{aligned}

Let's now consider each of the given equivalence classes.

- $3\notin [0]$ because $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 0)=1\ne -1\,\times $

- $3\in [1]$ because $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 1)=-1\,✓$

- $3\notin [2]$ because $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 2)=1\ne -1\,\times $

$$

$$

All of the elements of $A$ have been placed into an equivalence class, so we are done.

We have $2$ distinct equivalence classes:

$$

$$"] ["question-d047cc89-db39-59a7-988f-ed7cc91aeaba" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-4ae4ef16-e79e-5d40-a0c5-0776f84027eb" :answer-field/id #uuid "answer-field-d8ae37cc-586d-5f42-83a1-41443720bcf7"] [17592186152258 :knowledge-point/questions "question-d77f9f0f-9817-528d-99c4-631fe49372a3"] [17592186153457 :tutorial/content "Recall that the residue class of $a$ modulo $n,$ denoted $[a]_n,$ is the set of integers that are congruent to $a$ modulo $n.$

$$
[a]_n = \big\{ x \in \mathbb{Z} \: | \: x \equiv a \,  \: (\text{mod}\:n) \big\}
$$

For example:

- The residue class of $0$ modulo $2$ corresponds to the even integers because all even integers have a remainder of $0$ when divided by $2.$

$$
\begin{aligned}[0]_{2}={0,\,\pm 2,\,\pm 4,\,…}\end{aligned}
$$

- On the other hand, the residue class of $1$ modulo $2$ corresponds to the odd integers because all odd integers have a remainder of $1$ when divided by $2.$

$$
\begin{aligned}[1]_{2}={\,\pm 1,\,\pm 3,\,\pm 5,\,…}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the residue classes $[0]_2$ and $[1]_2$ *partition* the integers, meaning that any integer belongs either to $[0]_2$ or $[1]_2,$ but never both.

![](images/89/8932542ec22de980b3b2e1a5a11a3edf2250efc7ea4f1ca64ca35aa4031c63c9.png)"] [17592186153458 :tutorial/content "A residue class is a particular type of a more general object called an **equivalence class.**

Given an equivalence relation $\sim$ on a set $A,$ the equivalence class of an element $a \in A,$ denoted $[a],$ consists of all the elements of $A$ that are equivalent to $a.$

$$
[a] = \{ x \in A \, | \, x \sim a \}
$$

Since any equivalence relation is symmetric, we can also write

$$
[a] = \{ x \in A \, | \, a \sim x \}.
$$

For example, consider the equivalence relation $\sim$ on $\mathbb{Z}$ defined by $a \sim b$ if and only if $|a|=|b|.$ 

Under this relation, two integers are equivalent if they have the same absolute value. The first few equivalence classes are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[0] & ={a\in Z∣a∼0} \\  & ={a\in Z∣|a|=|0|} \\  & ={a\in Z∣|a|=0} \\  & ={0} \\  \\ [1] & ={a\in Z∣a∼1} \\  & ={a\in Z∣|a|=|1|} \\  & ={a\in Z∣|a|=1} \\  & ={\pm 1} \\  \\ [2] & ={a\in Z∣a∼2} \\  & ={a\in Z∣|a|=|2|} \\  & ={a\in Z∣|a|=2} \\  & ={\pm 2} \\  \\ [3] & ={a\in Z∣a∼3} \\  & ={a\in Z∣|a|=|3|} \\  & ={a\in Z∣|a|=3} \\  & ={\pm 3} \\  & \,⋮\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- Equivalence relations can have a finite or infinite number of equivalence classes. This particular equivalence relation has an infinite number of equivalence classes.

- For equivalence classes containing more than one element, we can use any element to represent the class. For example, $[1]$ and $[-1]$ represent the same equivalence class."] [17592186153480 :tutorial/content "The properties of residue classes generalize to equivalence classes. Let's list some of them:

- If $a \sim b$ then $[a]=[b].$ This allows us to pick any element of a class as its representative.

- On the other hand, two distinct equivalence classes have an empty intersection: 

$$
a \not\sim b
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
[a] \cap [b] = \emptyset
$$

- The residue classes form a partition of $A.$ Moreover, $A$ can be constructed from the (disjoint) union of all distinct equivalence classes:

$$
A = \bigcup_{i\in I}\,[a]_i
$$

where $[a]_i$ denotes the $i$'th residue class and $I$ is an index set spanning all possible classes.

Consider once again the equivalence relation $\sim$ on $\mathbb{Z}$ defined by $a \sim b$ if and only if $|a|=|b|.$ We found that the equivalence classes were as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[0] & ={0} \\ [1] & ={\pm 1} \\ [2] & ={\pm 2} \\ [3] & ={\pm 3} \\  & ⋮\end{aligned}
$$

These equivalence classes form a partition of the set of integers:

$$
\big\{[0], [1], [2],\ldots\big\}
$$

Moreover, the integers can be constructed from the disjoint union of these classes:

$$
\begin{aligned}Z & =[0]\cup [1]\cup [2]\cup ⋯ \\  & ={0}\cup {\pm 1}\cup {\pm 2}\cup ⋯\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186152337 :activity/expected-seconds 660.0]] "retractions" [[17592186151849 :question/problem "Consider the equivalence relation $\sim$ on $\mathbb{Z}$, defined by $x \sim y$ if $12 \, \mid \, (x-y)$. Which of the following are in the equivalence class $[9]$?

1. $9$
2. $21$
3. $22$"] [17592186151849 :question/worked-solution "The equivalence class $[9]$ consists of the elements that are equivalent to $9$ under the given equivalence relation. So, we have

$$

&= {x ∈ Z: 12 \mid (x - 9)} \\
&= {x ∈ Z: x = 9 + 12k, k ∈ Z} \\
&= {…,-15,-3, 9, 21, 33, …}
\end{aligned}
$$

We see that $9$ and $21$ are in $[9]$, while $22$ is not.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only.""] [17592186151851 :question/problem "Consider the equivalence relation $\sim$ on $\mathbb{R}$, defined by $x \sim y$ if $\sin x = \sin y$. Which of the following equivalence classes contain the element $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$?

$$

For example:

- The residue class of $0$ modulo $2$ corresponds to the even integers because all even integers have a remainder of $0$ when divided by $2$.
$[0]_{2} = {0, ± 2, ± 4, …}$
- On the other hand, the residue class of $1$ modulo $2$ corresponds to the odd integers because all odd integers have a remainder of $1$ when divided by $2$.
$[1]_{2} = {± 1, ± 3, ± 5, …}$

![](images/89/8932542ec22de980b3b2e1a5a11a3edf2250efc7ea4f1ca64ca35aa4031c63c9.png)"] [17592186153458 :tutorial/content "A residue class is a particular type of a more general object called an **equivalence class.**

Given an equivalence relation $\sim$ on a set $A$, the equivalence class of an element $a \in A$, denoted $[a]$, consists of all the elements of $A$ that are equivalent to $a$.

$$
[a] = \{x \in A \, \mid \, x \sim a \}
$$

Since any equivalence relation is symmetric, we can also write

$$
[a] = \{x \in A \, \mid \, a \sim x \}
$$

For example, consider the equivalence relation $\sim$ on $\mathbb{Z}$ defined by $a \sim b$ if and only if

$$
\begin{aligned}
\begin{vmatrix}a &= & b\end{vmatrix}
\end{aligned}
$$

Under this relation, two integers are equivalent if they have the same absolute value. The first few equivalence classes are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
[0] &= {a ∈ Z∣a∼0} \\
= {a ∈ Z∣\begin{vmatrix}a &= & 0\end{vmatrix}} \\
= {a ∈ Z∣\begin{vmatrix}a &= 0} \\ = {0} \\ [1]|= {a ∈ Z∣a∼1} \\ = {a ∈ Z∣\begin{vmatrix}a|= & 1\end{vmatrix}} \\ = {a ∈ Z∣ \mid a|= 1} \\ = {± 1} \\ [2]|= {a ∈ Z∣a∼2} \\ = {a ∈ Z∣\begin{vmatrix}a|= & 2\end{vmatrix}} \\ = {a ∈ Z∣ \mid a|= 2} \\ = {± 2} \\ [3]|= {a ∈ Z∣a∼3} \\ = {a ∈ Z∣\begin{vmatrix}a|= & 3\end{vmatrix}} \\ = {a ∈ Z∣\end{vmatrix}a|= 3} \\
&= {± 3} \\
&= ⋮
\end{aligned}
$$

- On the other hand, two distinct equivalence classes have an empty intersection:
$a \not\sim b \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad [a] \cap [b] = \emptyset$
- The residue classes form a partition of $A$. Moreover, $A$ can be constructed from the (disjoint) union of all distinct equivalence classes:
$A = \bigcup_{i\in I}\,[a]_i$
where $[a]_i$ denotes the $i$'th residue class and $I$ is an index set spanning all possible classes.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\begin{vmatrix}a &= & b\end{vmatrix}
\end{aligned}
$$

We found that the equivalence classes were as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
[0] &= {0} \\
[1] &= {± 1} \\
[2] &= {± 2} \\
[3] &= {± 3} \\
&= ⋮
\end{aligned}
$$

These equivalence classes form a partition of the set of integers:
$\big\{[0], [1], [2],\ldots\big\}$

Moreover, the integers can be constructed from the disjoint union of these classes:

$$
\begin{aligned}
Z &= [0]∪[1]∪[2]∪⋯ \\
&= {0}∪{± 1}∪{± 2}∪⋯
\end{aligned}
$$"]]}

$$
[a]_n = \big\{x \in \mathbb{Z} \: \mid \: x \equiv a \, \: (\text{mod}\:n) \big\}
$$

For example:

- The residue class of $0$ modulo $2$ corresponds to the even integers because all even integers have a remainder of $0$ when divided by $2$.
$[0]_{2} = {0, ± 2, ± 4, …}$
- On the other hand, the residue class of $1$ modulo $2$ corresponds to the odd integers because all odd integers have a remainder of $1$ when divided by $2$.
$[1]_{2} = {± 1, ± 3, ± 5, …}$

Notice that the residue classes $[0]_2$ and $[1]_2$ *partition* the integers, meaning that any integer belongs either to $[0]_2$ or $[1]_2$, but never both.

![](images/89/8932542ec22de980b3b2e1a5a11a3edf2250efc7ea4f1ca64ca35aa4031c63c9.png)" 17592186045417] [17592186153457 1065 9029 17592186045417] [17592186153457 1066 #uuid "33bb31fa-3552-5d74-b6fc-efc1bc68b367" 17592186045417] [17592186153457 1067 "Introduction" 17592186045417] [17592186153458 1064 "A residue class is a particular type of a more general object called an **equivalence class.**

Given an equivalence relation $\sim$ on a set $A$, the equivalence class of an element $a \in A$, denoted $[a]$, consists of all the elements of $A$ that are equivalent to $a$.

$$
[a] = \{x \in A \, \mid \, x \sim a \}
$$

Since any equivalence relation is symmetric, we can also write

$$
[a] = \{x \in A \, \mid \, a \sim x \}
$$

For example, consider the equivalence relation $\sim$ on $\mathbb{Z}$ defined by $a \sim b$ if and only if

$$
\begin{aligned}
\begin{vmatrix}a &= & b\end{vmatrix}
\end{aligned}
$$

Under this relation, two integers are equivalent if they have the same absolute value. The first few equivalence classes are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
[0] &= {a ∈ Z∣a∼0} \\
= {a ∈ Z∣\begin{vmatrix}a &= & 0\end{vmatrix}} \\
= {a ∈ Z∣\begin{vmatrix}a &= 0} \\ = {0} \\ [1]|= {a ∈ Z∣a∼1} \\ = {a ∈ Z∣\begin{vmatrix}a|= & 1\end{vmatrix}} \\ = {a ∈ Z∣ \mid a|= 1} \\ = {± 1} \\ [2]|= {a ∈ Z∣a∼2} \\ = {a ∈ Z∣\begin{vmatrix}a|= & 2\end{vmatrix}} \\ = {a ∈ Z∣ \mid a|= 2} \\ = {± 2} \\ [3]|= {a ∈ Z∣a∼3} \\ = {a ∈ Z∣\begin{vmatrix}a|= & 3\end{vmatrix}} \\ = {a ∈ Z∣\end{vmatrix}a|= 3} \\
&= {± 3} \\
&= ⋮
\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- Equivalence relations can have a finite or infinite number of equivalence classes. This particular equivalence relation has an infinite number of equivalence classes.
- For equivalence classes containing more than one element, we can use any element to represent the class. For example, $[1]$ and $[-1]$ represent the same equivalence class." 17592186045417] [17592186153458 1065 9030 17592186045417] [17592186153458 1066 #uuid "67a56179-d17e-54ab-86a3-aeca86ce5a7d" 17592186045417] [17592186153458 1067 "Equivalence Classes" 17592186045417] [17592186153480 1064 "The properties of residue classes generalize to equivalence classes. Let's list some of them:

- If $a \sim b$ then $[a]=[b]$. This allows us to pick any element of a class as its representative.
- On the other hand, two distinct equivalence classes have an empty intersection:
$a \not\sim b \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad [a] \cap [b] = \emptyset$
- The residue classes form a partition of $A$. Moreover, $A$ can be constructed from the (disjoint) union of all distinct equivalence classes:
$A = \bigcup_{i\in I}\,[a]_i$
where $[a]_i$ denotes the $i$'th residue class and $I$ is an index set spanning all possible classes.

Consider once again the equivalence relation $\sim$ on $\mathbb{Z}$ defined by $a \sim b$ if and only if

$$
\begin{aligned}
\begin{vmatrix}a &= & b\end{vmatrix}
\end{aligned}
$$

We found that the equivalence classes were as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
[0] &= {0} \\
[1] &= {± 1} \\
[2] &= {± 2} \\
[3] &= {± 3} \\
&= ⋮
\end{aligned}
$$

These equivalence classes form a partition of the set of integers:
$\big\{[0], [1], [2],\ldots\big\}$

Moreover, the integers can be constructed from the disjoint union of these classes:

$$
\begin{aligned}
Z &= [0]∪[1]∪[2]∪⋯ \\
&= {0}∪{± 1}∪{± 2}∪⋯
\end{aligned}
$$" 17592186045417] [17592186153480 1065 9358 17592186045417] [17592186153480 1066 #uuid "6f51d5c2-6cda-51cd-9f6f-70d3f573d73b" 17592186045417] [17592186153480 1067 "Properties of Equivalence Classes" 17592186045417]]}
